course.title: Cloud Computing with AWS
course.tagline: Launch servers, store files and deploy apps on Amazon Web Services, step by step.

days.title: What Cloud Computing Is
days.goal: Understand what the cloud is and why companies use it.

video.title: AWS for Beginners Full Course

steps: Write down three things you use that run in the cloud: email, streaming, storage.
Learn the three cloud models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, in plain words.
Learn the five benefits of the cloud: pay as you go, scale up, no hardware, fast to start, available everywhere.
Compare buying a server with renting one in the cloud.
days.task: Write a short note: what the cloud is, in your own words, and one example of each model.
days.challenge: Find one company that moved to the cloud and write down why.

options: Using computers over the internet instead of owning your own machines
quiz.explain: Cloud computing means renting computers, storage and services over the internet, instead of buying and running your own.

quiz.q: What does 'pay as you go' mean?
options: You pay only for what you use, like electricity
quiz.explain: Pay as you go means you are billed for what you actually use, so you do not pay for idle machines.

quiz.q: What is the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS?
options: IaaS rents machines, PaaS rents a platform to build on, SaaS rents finished software
quiz.explain: IaaS gives you machines. PaaS gives you a platform to run code on. SaaS gives you ready software like Gmail.

days.title: Your AWS Account and the Free Tier
days.goal: Create an AWS account and understand what is free.

video.title: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Study Course

steps: Go to aws.amazon.com and create a free account with your email.
Set up a strong password and turn on MFA for the root user.
Open the Billing page and set a budget alert at $0 so you are warned if you spend anything.
Open the AWS Management Console and find the EC2, S3 and IAM services.
days.task: Create your AWS account, turn on MFA and set a $0 budget alert.
days.challenge: List the three services you found and what each one does.

quiz.q: What is the AWS Free Tier?
options: A set of AWS services you can use free for 12 months, within limits
quiz.explain: The Free Tier gives you limited free use of many services for a year, so you can learn without paying.

quiz.q: Why turn on MFA for the root user?
options: Because the root user can do anything, including spending money, so it needs the strongest protection
quiz.explain: The root user has full power over the account. MFA adds a second lock so a stolen password is not enough.

options: So AWS warns you the moment you start spending, before the bill grows
quiz.explain: A $0 alert warns you early. Cloud bills can grow fast if you leave services running.

days.title: The AWS Console and Regions
days.goal: Find your way around the AWS Console and pick the right region.

video.title: AWS Networking Full Course in 2 Hours (FREE)

steps: Open the console and use the search bar to find a service by name.
Change your region to one near you, like eu-west-1 (Ireland).
Learn what a region is: a separate AWS data centre location.
Check that a service you create lives in the region you picked.
days.task: Change your region, find three services with the search bar and write down what they do.
days.challenge: Explain in one sentence why you would pick a region near your users.

options: A separate geographic area with its own AWS data centres
quiz.explain: A region is a location, like Ireland or Virginia, where AWS runs data centres. You pick one per service.

options: Because it affects speed for your users, price and which services are available
quiz.explain: A region near your users is faster. Prices and available services also differ by region.

options: A separate data centre inside a region, so one failure does not take everything down
quiz.explain: Each region has several Availability Zones. Spreading across them keeps your app up when one fails.

days.title: IAM: Users, Groups and Permissions
days.goal: Understand IAM and why you should never use the root user daily.

video.title: AWS Lambda Tutorial for Beginners: Python Function, Test Events, Logs

steps: Learn what IAM is: it controls who can do what in your AWS account.
Create an IAM user for yourself with a password and MFA.
Put the user in a group and give the group a simple permission.
Log in as the IAM user and check what you can and cannot do.
days.task: Create an IAM user for daily work and stop using the root user.
days.challenge: Write down the difference between the root user and an IAM user.

options: Identity and Access Management: the service that controls who can do what in AWS
quiz.explain: IAM manages users, groups and permissions. It decides who can use which AWS service.

quiz.q: Why not use the root user every day?
options: Because root can do anything, including deleting the account, so a mistake or a leak is catastrophic
quiz.explain: Root has unlimited power. Daily work should use an IAM user with only the permissions it needs.

quiz.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
options: Give each user only the permissions they need, nothing more
quiz.explain: Least privilege means giving the smallest set of permissions that still lets someone do their job.

days.title: IAM Policies and Roles
days.goal: Write simple policies and use roles to give permissions safely.

video.title: Launch Your First AWS EC2 Instance: Key Pair, Security Group, SSH & Apache

steps: Read a simple JSON policy and identify what it allows.
Attach a managed policy like AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess to your user.
Create a role that lets an EC2 server read from S3.
Test that your user can read S3 but cannot delete a bucket.
days.task: Write a policy that allows listing S3 buckets but not deleting them.
days.challenge: Explain in one sentence what a role is and when you would use one.

options: A document that says what is allowed or denied, written in JSON
quiz.explain: A policy is a JSON document that lists what actions are allowed or denied on which resources.

options: A set of permissions that a service or a person can take on temporarily
quiz.explain: A role is a bundle of permissions that AWS services or people assume when they need it, then give back.

quiz.q: Why use a role instead of a user's keys on a server?
options: Because roles give temporary permissions with no long-lived keys to steal
quiz.explain: Roles give short-lived permissions. Storing a user's keys on a server is risky because keys can be stolen.

days.title: S3: Your First Bucket
days.goal: Create an S3 bucket and upload your first file.

video.title: AWS IAM Tutorial for Beginners | Users, Groups, Roles & Policies Explained

steps: Open S3 in the console and create a bucket with a unique name.
Pick your region and leave the defaults on, including Block Public Access.
Upload a file to the bucket.
Download the file back and check it is the same.
days.task: Create a bucket, upload three files and download one to check it works.
days.challenge: Write down your bucket's name and region.

options: Simple Storage Service: unlimited file storage in the cloud
quiz.explain: S3 stores files, called objects, in buckets. It is cheap, durable and can hold any amount of data.

options: A container in S3 that holds your files, with a name that must be unique worldwide
quiz.explain: A bucket is a container for files in S3. Its name must be unique across all of AWS.

quiz.q: Why leave Block Public Access on?
options: So your files are private by default and cannot be seen by strangers
quiz.explain: Block Public Access keeps your bucket private. You open only what you choose to share.

days.title: Project 1: Static Website on S3
days.goal: Host a simple website on S3 and share its link.

video.title: IAM Roles Explained: Why 'Switch Role' Fails (And How to Fix It) | AWS Hands-On #04

steps: Make a small website with an index.html file and a picture.
Upload the files to a bucket and turn on static website hosting.
Make the files public with a bucket policy that allows reading only.
Open the website link in your browser and share it with one person.
days.task: Finish the S3 website and open it on your phone to check it loads.
days.challenge: Add a second page and link it from the first.

quiz.q: What is static website hosting on S3?
options: S3 serving your HTML files as a website, with no server to run
quiz.explain: S3 can serve a website made of plain HTML, CSS and images, with no server code needed.

quiz.q: Why use a bucket policy for a public website?
options: To allow the public to read the files while keeping the bucket itself safe
quiz.explain: A bucket policy opens read access to the files, so anyone can view the site, while write access stays private.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a static and a dynamic website?
options: A static site shows the same files to everyone, a dynamic site builds pages per user
quiz.explain: Static sites serve fixed files. Dynamic sites run code to build pages for each visitor.

project.title: Static Website on S3
project.brief: Build a small website with an index.html file and a picture, upload it to an S3 bucket with static website hosting on, make the files public with a read-only bucket policy, and share the live link.
checks: An S3 bucket exists with a unique name.
Static website hosting is turned on.
The site has at least two pages linked together.
A bucket policy allows the public to read the files only.
The website loads in a browser on your phone.
Block Public Access is set correctly for the site to work.

days.title: EC2: Your First Virtual Server
days.goal: Launch your first EC2 server in the cloud.

video.title: Build Your First AWS EC2 Server in under 15 Mins (Free Tier + $20 Credit!)

steps: Open EC2 and click Launch Instance.
Pick Amazon Linux and a free tier instance type like t2.micro.
Create a key pair and download the .pem file somewhere safe.
Launch the instance and wait for it to show as running.
days.task: Launch an EC2 instance and check it is running in the console.
days.challenge: Write down your instance's public IP address.

options: Elastic Compute Cloud: virtual servers you rent in the cloud
quiz.explain: EC2 gives you virtual computers in the cloud. You pick the size, launch it and use it like a real server.

options: The size of the server: how much CPU and memory it has
quiz.explain: An instance type sets the server's power. t2.micro is small and free tier eligible; bigger types cost more.

options: A pair of keys used to log into your server securely instead of a password
quiz.explain: A key pair is a private key you keep and a public key AWS puts on the server. You log in with the private key.

days.title: Connecting to EC2 with SSH
days.goal: Connect to your server with SSH and run commands on it.

video.title: AWS Lambda with EventBridge Service | Step-by-Step Tutorial

steps: Open a terminal and connect with ssh -i your-key.pem ec2-user@your-ip.
Run whoami and pwd to check you are on the server.
Update the server with sudo yum update.
Install a web server with sudo yum install httpd and start it.
days.task: Connect to your server, install a web server and open your server's IP in a browser.
days.challenge: Write down the commands you used.

options: Secure Shell: a way to log into a remote computer securely over the internet
quiz.explain: SSH lets you log into a server and run commands on it, with the connection encrypted.

quiz.q: Why use a key instead of a password for SSH?
options: Because a key is much harder to guess or steal than a password
quiz.explain: Keys are long and random. Passwords can be guessed or brute forced; keys cannot be guessed.

options: A firewall for your EC2 instance that controls which traffic can reach it
quiz.explain: A security group is a virtual firewall. It decides which ports and IPs can reach your server.

days.title: Security Groups and Firewalls
days.goal: Control who can reach your server with security groups.

video.title: AWS S3 Storage Classes Tutorial | S3 Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier & Deep Archive

steps: Open your instance's security group in the console.
Allow SSH (port 22) only from your IP address.
Allow HTTP (port 80) from anywhere so people can see your website.
Test that your website loads in a browser.
days.task: Lock down your security group so SSH only works from your IP.
days.challenge: Explain in one sentence what a security group does.

quiz.q: What does a security group do?
options: It acts as a firewall, controlling which traffic can reach your EC2 instance
quiz.explain: A security group is a virtual firewall for your instance. You set rules for which ports and IPs are allowed.

quiz.q: Why allow SSH only from your IP?
options: So attackers cannot even try to log in from anywhere else
quiz.explain: Limiting SSH to your IP blocks login attempts from the rest of the internet.
Port 80 is the standard port for unencrypted web traffic. Port 443 is for HTTPS.

days.title: S3 Storage Classes and Lifecycle
days.goal: Save money by picking the right storage class for each file.

video.title: AWS for Beginners Full Course

steps: Learn the main S3 storage classes: Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier and Deep Archive.
Check the price difference between Standard and Glacier.
Set a lifecycle rule that moves old files to a cheaper class.
Set a rule that deletes files in a temporary folder after 30 days.
days.task: Set a lifecycle rule on your bucket that moves files older than 90 days to Glacier.
days.challenge: Write down which storage class you would pick for backups and why.

quiz.q: What is an S3 storage class?
options: A tier that sets the price and how fast you can get your files back
quiz.explain: Storage classes trade price against access speed. Standard is fast and pricier; Glacier is cheap and slow to retrieve.

options: A class that moves your files between tiers automatically based on how often you use them
quiz.explain: Intelligent-Tiering watches how often you access each file and moves it to the cheapest tier that fits.

options: A rule that moves or deletes files automatically when they reach a certain age
quiz.explain: Lifecycle rules automate storage: move old files to cheaper storage or delete temporary files after a set time.

days.title: CloudFront: Delivering Content Fast
days.goal: Speed up your website with CloudFront, AWS's content delivery network.

video.title: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Study Course

steps: Learn what a CDN does: it copies your files to servers near your users.
Create a CloudFront distribution for your S3 website.
Open your site through the CloudFront link and check it loads.
Compare the load time with the direct S3 link.
days.task: Put your S3 website behind CloudFront and share the new link.
days.challenge: Write down one benefit of using a CDN.

options: A content delivery network: servers around the world that cache your files close to users
quiz.explain: A CDN copies your files to edge servers near your users, so pages load fast no matter where they are.
CloudFront is AWS's content delivery network. It serves your content from the nearest edge location.

quiz.q: Why use a CDN for a website?
options: So users far from your bucket still get fast load times
quiz.explain: A CDN puts copies near users, so a visitor in another country does not wait for data to cross the world.

days.title: Databases on AWS: RDS
days.goal: Run a managed database with Amazon RDS.

video.title: AWS Networking Full Course in 2 Hours (FREE)

steps: Learn what RDS is: a managed database service that handles backups and updates.
Create a free tier MySQL database with RDS.
Set a master username and password and keep them safe.
Connect to the database from your EC2 instance.
days.task: Create an RDS MySQL database and connect to it from your computer.
days.challenge: Write down the endpoint address of your database.

options: Relational Database Service: managed databases in the cloud
quiz.explain: RDS runs your database for you: it handles setup, backups, updates and scaling.

options: So you do not have to install, patch or back up the database yourself
quiz.explain: A managed database removes the boring work: AWS handles backups, patches and hardware.

options: The address your app uses to connect to the database
quiz.explain: The endpoint is the hostname and port your app connects to when it talks to the database.

days.title: Project 2: Deploy a Website on EC2
days.goal: Deploy a real website on an EC2 server with a database.

video.title: AWS Lambda Tutorial for Beginners: Python Function, Test Events, Logs

steps: Launch an EC2 instance and install a web server on it.
Upload your website files to the server.
Create an RDS database and connect your website to it.
Open the website in a browser and check it loads with data from the database.
days.task: Finish the deployment and share the website link with one person.
days.challenge: Write down the steps you took, in order.

options: Putting your website on a server so others can visit it
quiz.explain: Deploying means moving your code onto a server and starting it, so the world can reach it.

quiz.q: Why use a separate database server?
options: So the database can be backed up and scaled on its own, apart from the web server
quiz.explain: Separating the database lets you back it up, scale it and protect it independently of the web server.

quiz.q: What should you check after deploying?
options: That the site loads, the data shows, and the server is secure
quiz.explain: After deploying, check the site works, the data loads, and the security group only allows what it should.

project.title: Deploy a Website on EC2
project.brief: Launch an EC2 instance, install a web server, upload your website files, create an RDS database and connect the website to it, then open the site in a browser and check it loads with data from the database.
checks: An EC2 instance is running.
A web server is installed and serving your site.
An RDS database exists and the site connects to it.
The security group allows HTTP and SSH only from your IP.
The website loads in a browser with data from the database.
You can list the steps you took, in order.

days.title: Lambda: Serverless Functions
days.goal: Run code without a server using AWS Lambda.

video.title: Launch Your First AWS EC2 Instance: Key Pair, Security Group, SSH & Apache

steps: Learn what serverless means: you write code, AWS runs it when something happens.
Create a Lambda function in Python that returns 'Hello from Lambda'.
Test the function in the console.
Trigger it with a test event and read the logs.
days.task: Create a Lambda function that greets you by name and test it.
days.challenge: Write down one job Lambda is good for.

options: A service that runs your code when triggered, with no server to manage
quiz.explain: Lambda runs your code in response to events, like an upload or a schedule. You never manage a server.

options: You write code and the cloud provider runs it, without you managing servers
quiz.explain: Serverless means no server for you to run. The provider handles the machines and scales your code automatically.

options: Events like a file upload, a schedule, or an HTTP request
quiz.explain: Lambda runs when something happens: a file is uploaded, a timer fires, or a request arrives.

days.title: EventBridge and Automation
days.goal: Automate jobs with EventBridge schedules and events.

video.title: AWS IAM Tutorial for Beginners | Users, Groups, Roles & Policies Explained

steps: Create an EventBridge rule that runs your Lambda function every hour.
Check the logs to confirm it ran.
Make a rule that triggers when a file is uploaded to S3.
Turn the rule off when you are done.
days.task: Set up a scheduled Lambda that runs once a day and writes a log message.
days.challenge: Write down two jobs you would automate with a schedule.

options: AWS's service for schedules and events that trigger other services
quiz.explain: EventBridge routes events and runs schedules. It connects services so one thing can trigger another.

options: To run regular jobs, like a daily report or cleanup, without a server running all the time
quiz.explain: A scheduled Lambda runs a job on time, then stops. You pay only for the seconds it runs.

options: A design where things happen in response to events, not on a fixed schedule
quiz.explain: Event-driven means work happens when something changes, like a file upload, instead of polling all the time.

days.title: VPC and Networking Basics
days.goal: Understand how AWS networking works with VPCs.

video.title: IAM Roles Explained: Why 'Switch Role' Fails (And How to Fix It) | AWS Hands-On #04

steps: Learn what a VPC is: your own private network inside AWS.
Learn what subnets are: smaller networks inside a VPC.
Create a VPC with a public subnet and a private subnet.
Put your web server in the public subnet and your database in the private one.
days.task: Draw a simple diagram of your VPC with public and private subnets.
days.challenge: Explain in one sentence why the database goes in the private subnet.

options: Virtual Private Cloud: your own isolated network inside AWS
quiz.explain: A VPC is your private network in AWS. You control its addresses, subnets and who can reach it.

options: A smaller network inside a VPC, like a public or private section
quiz.explain: A subnet is a slice of your VPC. Public subnets can reach the internet; private ones cannot.

quiz.q: Why put the database in a private subnet?
options: So the internet cannot reach it directly. Only your app server can
quiz.explain: A database in a private subnet has no public address, so attackers on the internet cannot connect to it directly.

days.title: Monitoring with CloudWatch
days.goal: Watch your services and get alerted when something goes wrong.

video.title: Build Your First AWS EC2 Server in under 15 Mins (Free Tier + $20 Credit!)

steps: Open CloudWatch and look at the CPU graph for your EC2 instance.
Create an alarm that warns you when CPU goes above 80%.
Read the logs from your Lambda function in CloudWatch Logs.
Set up an alarm that emails you when something breaks.
days.task: Create a CloudWatch alarm for high CPU on your instance.
days.challenge: Find one error in your Lambda logs and write down what it says.

options: AWS's monitoring service: metrics, logs and alarms
quiz.explain: CloudWatch collects numbers and logs from your services and can warn you when something is wrong.

options: A number that shows how a service is doing, like CPU use or requests per minute
quiz.explain: A metric is a measurement over time, like CPU percent or how many requests your site got.

options: A rule that sends a message when a metric crosses a limit you set
quiz.explain: An alarm watches a metric and notifies you, by email or message, when it goes over your limit.

days.title: Costs and Billing
days.goal: Understand what AWS costs and how to keep the bill low.

video.title: AWS Lambda with EventBridge Service | Step-by-Step Tutorial

steps: Open the Billing dashboard and see what you have used.
Learn the three main costs: compute (EC2), storage (S3) and data transfer.
Find the Cost Explorer and see which service costs the most.
Stop or delete anything you are not using.
days.task: Check your bill, find your most expensive service, and stop anything you do not need.
days.challenge: Write down three ways to keep an AWS bill low.

quiz.q: What costs the most in AWS for beginners?
options: Usually EC2 servers left running, and data leaving AWS
quiz.explain: Servers left running and data transfer out are the usual surprise costs. Storage is usually cheap.

options: A tool that shows what you spent, on which service, over time
quiz.explain: Cost Explorer breaks down your spending by service and time, so you can see where the money goes.

quiz.q: How do you keep an AWS bill low?
options: Stop unused servers, use the right size, and set budget alerts
quiz.explain: Turn off what you do not use, pick the smallest size that works, and set alerts so surprises are caught early.

days.title: API Gateway: Let the World Call Your Lambda
days.goal: Put a public web address in front of your Lambda function with API Gateway.

video.title: AWS S3 Storage Classes Tutorial | S3 Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier & Deep Archive

steps: Learn what API Gateway does: it gives your function a URL anyone can call.
Create a REST API and connect it to your Lambda function.
Deploy the API and call its URL in a browser.
Check the response and read the logs.
days.task: Create an API for your Lambda function and call it from your browser.
days.challenge: Add a second route that returns a different message.

options: AWS's service that gives your code a public web address and handles requests for it
quiz.explain: API Gateway is the front door for your APIs. It takes web requests and passes them to your Lambda functions.

quiz.q: Why put API Gateway in front of Lambda?
options: So your function has a stable public URL and you can control who calls it
quiz.explain: Lambda alone has no public address. API Gateway gives it one and adds controls like limits and keys.

quiz.q: What is a route in API Gateway?
options: A URL path and method, like GET /hello, that maps to a function
quiz.explain: A route is a path plus a method. Each route points to the code that should answer it.

days.title: Project 3: Serverless App
days.goal: Build a serverless app with S3, Lambda and an API.

video.title: AWS for Beginners Full Course

steps: Make a simple web page hosted on S3.
Create a Lambda function that returns data as JSON.
Connect the page to the function so it shows live data.
Test the whole flow in a browser and check the logs.
days.task: Finish the serverless app and share the link with one person.
days.challenge: Write down the three services you used and what each one does.

options: It has no servers at all
It runs on services like S3 and Lambda, with no server for you to manage
quiz.explain: A serverless app uses managed services for everything, so there is no server for you to run or patch.

quiz.q: Why is serverless good for small apps?
options: Because you pay only when it runs, and it scales by itself
quiz.explain: Serverless scales automatically and you pay per use, which fits apps with uneven traffic.

quiz.q: What should you check after building a serverless app?
options: That the page loads, the function runs, and the logs show no errors
quiz.explain: Check the full flow: the page, the function and the logs, so you know every part works.

project.title: Serverless App
project.brief: Build a serverless app: a web page hosted on S3, a Lambda function that returns data as JSON, and a connection between them so the page shows live data. Test the whole flow in a browser and check the logs.
checks: A web page is hosted on S3.
A Lambda function returns data as JSON.
The page calls the function and shows live data.
The whole flow works in a browser.
CloudWatch logs show the function ran without errors.
You can name the three services used and what each does.

days.title: Security Best Practices on AWS
days.goal: Apply the security habits that keep an AWS account safe.

video.title: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Study Course

steps: Turn on MFA for the root user and for all IAM users.
Use roles instead of long-lived access keys where you can.
Enable CloudTrail so every action in your account is logged.
Review your security groups and close any port you do not need.
days.task: Do a security check on your account and fix the top three issues.
days.challenge: Write down your security rules for any future AWS account.

options: A service that logs every action taken in your AWS account
quiz.explain: CloudTrail records who did what and when in your account, which is vital for investigating problems.

options: Because a leaked key lets anyone act as that user until it is deleted
quiz.explain: Access keys are like passwords for programs. If one leaks, anyone can use it until you delete it.

quiz.q: What is the shared responsibility model?
options: AWS secures the cloud itself, and you secure what you put in it
quiz.explain: AWS secures the data centres and the services. You secure your data, your users and your settings.

days.title: Deploying with the AWS CLI
days.goal: Use the command line to work with AWS faster.

video.title: AWS Networking Full Course in 2 Hours (FREE)

steps: Install the AWS CLI on your computer.
Configure it with your IAM user's access key.
List your S3 buckets with aws s3 ls.
Upload a file to S3 from the terminal.
days.task: Upload your website to S3 using only the AWS CLI.
days.challenge: Write down the three commands you used most.

options: A command-line tool that lets you control AWS from your terminal
quiz.explain: The AWS CLI lets you run AWS actions from the terminal, which is faster for repeated jobs and scripts.

quiz.q: Why use the CLI instead of the console?
options: Because commands can be repeated, scripted and automated
quiz.explain: The console is good for learning. The CLI is good for doing the same job many times or in a script.

options: The command that sets up your access key, region and output format for the CLI
quiz.explain: aws configure stores your credentials and default region so the CLI knows which account to talk to.

days.title: Introduction to Terraform
days.goal: Describe your infrastructure as code with Terraform.

video.title: AWS Lambda Tutorial for Beginners: Python Function, Test Events, Logs

steps: Learn what infrastructure as code means: your servers and buckets written in files.
Install Terraform on your computer.
Write a small Terraform file that creates an S3 bucket.
Run terraform apply and check the bucket appears in the console.
days.task: Write a Terraform file that creates an S3 bucket and an EC2 instance.
days.challenge: Destroy the resources with terraform destroy and check they are gone.

options: Writing your servers, networks and buckets as files you can version and repeat
quiz.explain: Infrastructure as code means your cloud setup lives in files. You can review it, version it and recreate it exactly.

options: It creates or updates the resources described in your Terraform files
quiz.explain: terraform apply reads your files and makes the real cloud match them.

options: So you stop paying for things you no longer need
quiz.explain: Cloud resources cost money while they exist. Destroying test resources stops the bill.

days.title: Containers on AWS: ECS Basics
days.goal: Run a containerised app on AWS with ECS.

video.title: Launch Your First AWS EC2 Instance: Key Pair, Security Group, SSH & Apache

steps: Learn what a container is: a small package with your app and everything it needs.
Build a Docker image of a simple web app on your computer.
Push the image to Amazon ECR.
Run it on ECS Fargate and open it in a browser.
days.task: Run a simple container on ECS Fargate and open it in a browser.
days.challenge: Write down the difference between ECS and running a server yourself.

options: A package that holds your app and its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere
quiz.explain: A container bundles your app with everything it needs, so it runs the same on your laptop and in the cloud.

options: Elastic Container Registry: a place to store your Docker images
quiz.explain: ECR stores your container images privately so AWS services can pull and run them.

options: A way to run containers on AWS without managing any servers
quiz.explain: Fargate runs your containers for you. You do not pick or manage the machines underneath.

days.title: DynamoDB: NoSQL Database Basics
days.goal: Store data in DynamoDB, AWS's NoSQL database.

video.title: AWS IAM Tutorial for Beginners | Users, Groups, Roles & Policies Explained

steps: Learn the difference between a relational database and a NoSQL database.
Create a DynamoDB table with a partition key.
Add an item to the table in the console.
Read the item back and update one of its fields.
days.task: Create a DynamoDB table for your app's data and add five items to it.
days.challenge: Query the table for one item by its key.

options: AWS's fast NoSQL database that stores items as documents
quiz.explain: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database. It stores items without a fixed schema and scales to huge amounts of data.

quiz.q: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL?
options: SQL databases use tables with fixed columns, NoSQL stores flexible items without a fixed schema
SQL is for small data only
quiz.explain: SQL uses strict tables. NoSQL stores items that can have different fields, which fits fast-changing data.

options: The field DynamoDB uses to find and spread your items
quiz.explain: The partition key is how DynamoDB locates an item. Pick a key that spreads your data evenly.

days.title: Route 53 and Custom Domains
days.goal: Give your app a real domain name with Route 53.

video.title: IAM Roles Explained: Why 'Switch Role' Fails (And How to Fix It) | AWS Hands-On #04

steps: Learn what DNS does: it turns a name like example.com into an address.
Register a domain name in Route 53 or point one you own to AWS.
Create a record that points your domain to your CloudFront site.
Open your site with your own domain name in a browser.
days.task: Point a domain name at your S3 website and open it with the new name.
days.challenge: Write down the difference between an A record and a CNAME record.

options: AWS's DNS service: it turns domain names into addresses
quiz.explain: Route 53 is AWS's domain name service. It routes visitors to your app when they type your domain.

options: An entry that says where a name points, like which server an address belongs to
quiz.explain: A DNS record maps a name to an address. An A record points to an IP, a CNAME points to another name.

quiz.q: Why use your own domain name?
options: Because it looks professional and people can remember it
quiz.explain: A real domain name is easy to remember and looks trustworthy, unlike a long cloud address.

days.title: AWS Well-Architected Framework
days.goal: Check your cloud setup against AWS's six pillars of good design.

video.title: Build Your First AWS EC2 Server in under 15 Mins (Free Tier + $20 Credit!)

steps: Learn the six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance, cost and sustainability.
Check your project against the security pillar: MFA, least privilege, encryption.
Check it against the reliability pillar: backups, multiple zones, alarms.
Write down one improvement for each pillar.
days.task: Run a Well-Architected check on your capstone project and list six improvements.
days.challenge: Fix the easiest improvement on your list.

options: AWS's guide to building good cloud systems, organised into six pillars
quiz.explain: The framework is a checklist for cloud design. Each pillar covers one quality: security, reliability, cost and more.

options: So your app keeps working when a server or a data centre fails
quiz.explain: Reliability means your app survives failures: backups, multiple zones and alarms keep it up.

quiz.q: What does the cost pillar ask?
options: Use only what you need, pick the right size, and turn off what you do not use
quiz.explain: The cost pillar is about using the right resources and no more, so you never pay for idle capacity.

days.title: The AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Exam
days.goal: Prepare for the AWS Cloud Practitioner exam.

video.title: AWS Lambda with EventBridge Service | Step-by-Step Tutorial

steps: List the four exam domains and what each covers.
Rate yourself on each domain from 1 to 5.
Study your weakest domain for one hour.
Do twenty practice questions and check your answers.
days.task: Write your exam study plan with a date for each domain.
days.challenge: Do a full practice test and note your score.

quiz.q: What is the Cloud Practitioner exam?
options: AWS's entry-level certification that tests cloud concepts and AWS basics
quiz.explain: Cloud Practitioner is the first AWS certification. It tests cloud ideas, AWS services, security and billing.

options: So you spend study time on your weakest areas, not your strongest
quiz.explain: Rating yourself shows where to focus. Studying what you already know wastes time.

quiz.q: How should you use practice questions?
options: Do them, check why each answer is right or wrong, and learn the idea behind it
quiz.explain: Practice questions teach you the ideas. Understanding why an answer is right matters more than the score.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your Cloud Project
days.goal: Review everything, pick your capstone project and plan your demo.

video.title: AWS S3 Storage Classes Tutorial | S3 Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier & Deep Archive

steps: List the projects you built and pick the strongest one to finish.
Write a short plan: the problem, the services, the architecture and the demo.
Draw a simple diagram of your architecture.
Practise explaining your project in simple words, as if to a friend.
days.task: Write your capstone plan and a one-minute explanation of your project.
days.challenge: Show your architecture diagram to one person and note their questions.

quiz.q: What makes a good capstone cloud project?
options: A real problem solved with the right services, a clear diagram and a working demo
quiz.explain: A good capstone solves a real problem with services that fit, a clear diagram and a demo that works.

options: So anyone can see how the services connect at a glance
quiz.explain: A diagram shows the whole system in one picture: which services, how they connect, and where data flows.

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The problem, the services, the architecture and how you will show it
quiz.explain: A plan covers the problem, the services you will use, how they fit together and how you will present it.

capstone.title: Build and Deploy a Complete Cloud App
capstone.brief: Build a complete cloud application on AWS: a website hosted on S3 and CloudFront, a backend on EC2 or Lambda, a database on RDS, and monitoring with CloudWatch. Draw an architecture diagram, keep the bill near zero with the Free Tier, and present a live demo.
checks: The app solves a real problem and you can explain the problem in one sentence.
The frontend is hosted on S3 with CloudFront.
The backend runs on EC2 or Lambda.
Data is stored in RDS or DynamoDB.
CloudWatch monitors the app and an alarm exists.
An architecture diagram shows how the services connect.
You can present a live demo and explain how it works in simple words.
deliverables: A working cloud app with a live link.
An architecture diagram of the services used.
A README.md explaining the problem, the services and how to run it.
A short demo video or screenshots showing the app running.
A one-page write-up of what you learned in 30 days.
